mainTopic: A sick husband's conditional גט, the power of the רבנן to cancel קידושין, and whether accepting 'every accident' covers rare accidents
overview: The amud opens by finishing a discussion of a sick husband's conditional גט. An אומדנא about which illness killed him is needed only if he got up and walked with his cane. The גמרא then rules, with רבי אלעזר quoting רב, that a שכיב מרע who passed straight from one illness to another still gives a valid gift. Next, רבה and רבא reject רב הונא's rule because of a גזירה, and the גמרא explains how the רבנן can cancel even a Torah-level קידושין. A ברייתא about a husband who dies from a house collapse or a snakebite leads into the question of whether accepting 'every accident' includes rare accidents. Through a land-sale case, a challenge from that ברייתא, and a case of sailors on the נהר מלכא, רבא rules that rare accidents are not included. The amud ends with a new משנה: the wife holding such a גט may be alone with her husband only before witnesses. The משנה then asks what her status is in the waiting days, and רבי יהודה's answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Assessment is needed only if he walked with his cane
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains what the ברייתא teaches: an אומדנא is needed only when the husband got up and walked with his cane. If he went straight from one illness to the next, no assessment is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what the ברייתא is teaching us: only when he walked with his cane do we need an assessment. In the other case, where he never got up, we do not even need an assessment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is explaining what new point the ברייתא makes. Only when the husband had partly recovered and walked with a cane do we need to assess which illness killed him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he got up and walked, he might have died from a new illness, so we must assess whether the first illness caused his death. If he never got up and went straight into another illness, it is obvious that the first illness led to his death. In that case the גט works without any assessment.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it teaches us
His walking stick or cane
An assessment or estimate, here of which illness caused the death
The other case

phrases.english: And this is what it teaches us:
that where he walked with his cane,
that is when we need an assessment;
in the other case, we do not even need an assessment.
phrases.notes: The "other case" is a man who never got up at all and went straight from one sickness into the next.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the earlier discussion about what the ברייתא is adding.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifies the specific case the ברייתא is teaching about
steps.terutzMaskana: An אומדנא is needed only when he walked with his cane; going straight from illness to illness needs no assessment.

steps.title: Does this also apply to a sick man's gift?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether we can learn from this that a שכיב מרע who passed from one illness to another still has a valid מתנת שכיב מרע.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can you learn from this that if a dying person went from one illness to another, his gift is a valid gift?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks whether the rule from step 1 carries over to the laws of gifts. If a dying man passed from one illness straight into another and then died, does his deathbed gift count?
steps.deeperAnalysis: A מתנת שכיב מרע works only if he dies from that illness. Step 1 treats moving from illness to illness as one continuous sickness. The question is whether the same reasoning makes the gift valid.

keyTerms.meaning: Can you learn from this?
A person on his deathbed
Passed from one illness to another
His gift is a valid gift

phrases.english: Can you learn from this
that a dying person who passed from one illness to another illness,
his gift is a valid gift?

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁמְעַתְּ מִינַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the rule of step 1 and asks whether it applies to gifts.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether moving from illness to illness keeps a deathbed gift valid

steps.title: Yes, as רב taught
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers yes and backs this up with a teaching from רבי אלעזר in the name of רב: such a person's gift is valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes. רבי אלעזר said in the name of רב: a dying person who passed from one illness to another, his gift is a valid gift.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says yes and supports the answer with an explicit statement of רב, quoted by רבי אלעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's ruling matches the reasoning of step 1. Moving straight from one illness to another counts as one continuous sickness. So the man is treated as dying from his original illness, and the gift stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Yes
In the name of

steps.whatToRemember: A שכיב מרע who passes straight from one illness to another is treated as dying from the first illness. His deathbed gift is valid, and in the גט case no אומדנא is needed.

phrases.aramaic: אִין, דְּאָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב:
phrases.english: Yes, as Rabbi Elazar said in the name of Rav:
a dying person who passed from one illness to another illness,
his gift is a valid gift.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִין, דְּאָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes. רב rules explicitly that the gift is valid.

steps.title: רבה and רבא reject רב הונא's rule because of a decree
steps.stepSummary: רבה and רבא do not accept רב הונא's rule that a sick man's גט is cancelled if he recovers. They say there is a גזירה so that people will not think a גט can work after death.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה and רבא do not agree with רב הונא's teaching. This is because of a decree, lest people say there can be a גט after death.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports that רבה and רבא disagree with רב הונא. Their reason is a rabbinic גזירה: people might wrongly conclude that a גט can take effect after the husband dies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא says that if the sick husband recovers, the גט is automatically cancelled, as if it only took effect at his death. רבה and רבא worry this would look like a 'גט after death', which is invalid. So they rule against רב הונא and treat the גט as valid even if he recovers.

keyTerms.meaning: They do not hold this opinion
A rabbinic protective decree
Lest people say
A גט that takes effect after death, which is invalid

steps.confusionAlert: רבה and רבא are not arguing about what the Torah says. They agree with רב הונא's logic on Torah level. Their disagreement is only because of a rabbinic decree.

phrases.english: Rabba and Rava do not hold
this teaching of Rav Huna,
phrases.notes: This is רב הונא's rule from earlier: if the sick husband gets better, the גט falls away even if he never said so.

phrases.english: because of a decree, lest people say
there is a valid bill of divorce after death.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּה וְרָבָא לָא סְבִירָא לְהוּ הָא דְּרַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the earlier discussion of רב הונא's rule and presents a dissenting view.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבה and רבא reject רב הונא's rule because of a גזירה against people thinking a גט can work after death.

steps.title: Can a decree permit a married woman to remarry?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבה and רבא. If by Torah law the גט is not valid, how can a rabbinic decree allow a woman who is still an אשת איש to marry anyone?
steps.simpleTranslation: Is there really such a thing, where by Torah law the גט is not valid, and yet because of a decree we allow a married woman to marry anyone?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא strongly challenges רבה and רבא. A rabbinic decree should not be able to permit a woman who is still married by Torah law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By Torah law, the recovered husband's גט is cancelled, so she is still an אשת איש. Treating the גט as valid because of a decree would allow her to marry another man, which looks like permitting a real prohibition. The challenge is that a decree meant to be strict is producing a lenient result in a very serious area.

keyTerms.meaning: Is there really such a thing?
By Torah law
We permit
A married woman
To anyone, literally 'to the world'

steps.whyThisMatters: This raises a basic question: how far can rabbinic authority go in affecting whether a marriage has ended? The answer will shape how we understand רבה and רבא.

phrases.english: And is there really anything
that by Torah law is not a valid bill of divorce,
and because of a decree we permit
a married woman to marry anyone?!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אִיכָּא מִידֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reasoning of רבה and רבא from step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The גזירה of רבה and רבא that keeps the גט valid
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If on Torah level the גט is cancelled, a rabbinic decree cannot let a woman who is still married remarry.

steps.title: The רבנן can cancel the marriage because every marriage depends on them
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers yes. Every man marries based on the rules of the רבנן, so the רבנן can take the קידושין away from him, and the woman may remarry.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes. Anyone who marries a woman does it based on the rules of the רבנן, and the רבנן took the marriage away from him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 5. The רבנן really can free a woman who is married by Torah law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge asked how a rabbinic decree could let a married woman remarry. The answer is that every קידושין is made on condition that the רבנן agree. So when the רבנן cancel it, the marriage falls away from the start, and she was never really an אשת איש.

keyTerms.meaning: Based on the rules and agreement of the רבנן
They took it away or cancelled it (from the word הַפְקָעָה)
The first stage of Jewish marriage, which makes the woman an אשת איש

steps.whyThisMatters: This rule, that the רבנן can cancel a marriage, is a key idea that comes up in several places in ש״ס.

phrases.english: Yes, anyone who betroths a woman
betroths her based on the will of the Sages,
and the Sages took the betrothal away from him.
phrases.notes: He means the marriage is cancelled backwards, from the very beginning.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִין, כֹּל דִּמְקַדֵּשׁ אַדַּעְתָּא דְּרַבָּנַן מְקַדֵּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 5
steps.terutzResolutionType: Introduces a new mechanism: the רבנן cancel the marriage backwards
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A rabbinic decree cannot override a marriage that is valid by Torah law
steps.terutzMaskana: Every קידושין depends on the agreement of the רבנן, so they can cancel it backwards

steps.title: רבינא asks how this works for marriage through intercourse
steps.stepSummary: רבינא asks רב אשי a question. Cancelling the marriage makes sense when it was done with money. But if the marriage was done through ביאה, what can we say?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to רב אשי: This works if he married her with money. But if he married her through intercourse, what is there to say?
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא challenges the answer from Step 6. He says it only seems to work for one kind of קידושין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With money, it is easy to see how the רבנן could take the money away from its owner, which would undo the marriage. But קידושין done through ביאה uses no money that can be taken back. So it is unclear how the רבנן could undo it.

keyTerms.meaning: This works well (we can accept it in this case)
Money, one way of making קידושין
Intercourse, another way of making קידושין

phrases.english: Ravina said to Rav Ashi:
This works well where he betrothed her with money,
but if he betrothed her through intercourse,
what is there to say?

steps.triggerLanguage: תִּינַח דְּקַדֵּישׁ בְּכַסְפָּא, קַדֵּישׁ בְּבִיאָה מַאי אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how far the answer of Step 6 can reach
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the רבנן can cancel any קידושין
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Taking back money explains קידושין done with money, but a marriage through ביאה uses no money that can be taken back

steps.title: The רבנן turned the act into one that does not create marriage
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that the רבנן declared his intercourse to be בעילת זנות. Such an act does not create קידושין.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: The רבנן made his intercourse into intercourse that is not for marriage.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers רבינא's challenge. He explains how the רבנן cancel even a marriage done through ביאה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן do not need money to undo this kind of marriage. They give the act itself a new status: it counts as plain בעילת זנות and not as קידושין. So this marriage can also be cancelled.

keyTerms.meaning: They made it into or declared it to be
Intercourse that is not for marriage, which does not create קידושין

steps.whatToRemember: The רבנן can cancel any קידושין. With money, they take the money away. With ביאה, they declare the act to be בעילת זנות. This answers the challenge against רבה and רבא.

phrases.english: He said to him: The Sages declared
his intercourse to be licentious intercourse.

steps.triggerLanguage: שַׁוְּיוּהּ רַבָּנַן לִבְעִילָתוֹ בְּעִילַת זְנוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבינא's challenge in Step 7
steps.terutzResolutionType: Extends the same power to a different case through a different mechanism
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Marriage through ביאה cannot be cancelled because no money is involved
steps.terutzMaskana: The רבנן declare the act to be בעילת זנות, so it never created קידושין

steps.title: A sick man's conditional divorce when he dies from another cause
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא teaches two cases. If he said "if I die from this illness" and then died in a house collapse or from a snakebite, it is not a גט. If he said "if I do not get up from this illness" and died the same way, it is a גט.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: "This is your גט from today if I die from this illness," and a house fell on him or a snake bit him: it is not a גט. "If I do not get up from this illness," and a house fell on him or a snake bit him: it is a גט.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about a sick man who gives a גט with a condition, and two different wordings of that condition. This sets up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both cases the man did not die from his illness, and in both cases he also never got up healthy from it. Yet the ברייתא rules opposite ways for the two wordings. The next step asks what the difference is, and later the גמרא calls this ברייתא unreliable because its two halves contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: The רבנן taught, which introduces a ברייתא
From today, so the גט takes effect now and not after his death
Illness
I will get up, meaning recover

steps.confusionAlert: In both cases the man died from something else, not from his illness. The only difference between them is how he worded his condition.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
"This is your bill of divorce from today,
if I die from this illness,"
and the house collapsed on him
or a snake bit him, it is not a bill of divorce.
"If I will not get up from this illness,"
and a house collapsed on him

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ הִכִּישׁוֹ נָחָשׁ – הֲרֵי זֶה גֵּט.
phrases.english: or a snake bit him, this is a bill of divorce.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: זֶה גִּיטִּיךְ מֵהַיּוֹם, אִם מַתִּי מֵחוֹלִי זֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the discussion of רבה and רבא ends
steps.mimraCoreRuling: "If I die from this illness" followed by death from another cause: no גט. "If I do not get up from this illness" followed by death from another cause: valid גט.

steps.title: What is the difference between the two cases?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the two cases of the ברייתא have opposite rulings, since in both he did not die from his illness.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is different about the first case, and what is different about the second case?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the two halves of the ברייתא seem to contradict each other. No answer comes right here. Later, in steps 17–19, this same clash between the רישא and the סיפא leads to the conclusion that the ברייתא is faulty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both men died from a house collapse or a snakebite, not from their illness. Yet one גט is valid and the other is not. The גמרא wants to know what in the wording makes this difference.

keyTerms.meaning: What is different? (asking for the reason for two different rulings)
The first part of a teaching
The last part of a teaching

phrases.english: What is different in the first clause
and what is different in the latter clause?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי שְׁנָא רֵישָׁא וּמַאי שְׁנָא סֵיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the two different rulings of Step 9
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why "if I die from this illness" fails but "if I do not get up from this illness" works, when in both cases he died from another cause
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא of step 9, whose רישא and סיפא give opposite rulings for the same kinds of accidents

steps.title: A ruling from ארץ ישראל: if a lion ate him, there is no גט
steps.stepSummary: The scholars of ארץ ישראל sent a ruling: if a lion ate the husband, we do not treat the גט as valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: They sent a message from ארץ ישראל: if a lion ate him, we have nothing to worry about.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a new ruling to the ברייתא from Step 9. In the 'if I do not get up from this illness' case, if a lion ate him, the גט does not work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 9, a house falling or a snakebite still counted as 'not getting up,' so the גט took effect. A lion eating someone is far more unusual. So the ruling says the husband never had that in mind, and the גט is not valid.

keyTerms.meaning: They sent from there, meaning a ruling sent from the scholars of ארץ ישראל
A lion
We have nothing (to worry about), meaning the גט does not count

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a limit. Some unexpected deaths are covered by the husband's words, and some are too rare to count. That limit will matter in the land-sale story that follows.

phrases.english: They sent from there:
phrases.notes: 'There' is ארץ ישראל; this is how the scholars of בבל refer to rulings sent from there.

phrases.english: If a lion ate him, we have nothing (to be concerned about).
phrases.notes: He means the case of 'if I do not get up from this illness'. Here the גט does not take effect.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלַחוּ מִתָּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a further case to the ברייתא about 'if I do not get up from this illness'.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the husband is eaten by a lion, a death this rare is not included in his condition, so the גט does not take effect.

steps.title: A seller accepts every accident, and then a river is diverted through the field
steps.stepSummary: A man sold land and accepted responsibility for any accident that might happen to it. Later a river was diverted through the land.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a man who sold land to his friend and took upon himself every accident that might happen. In the end, a river was diverted through the land.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real-life story that sets up a legal question. Does the seller's promise cover even this unusual disaster?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The seller used a wide phrase: 'any accident that happens.' A river being diverted through the field is a real accident, but a strange one. The question is whether wide wording covers rare events too.

keyTerms.meaning: An accident beyond anyone's control
That may happen (literally, 'that is born')
They diverted a river into it
He took upon himself (accepted responsibility)

phrases.english: There was a certain man
who sold land to his friend,
he accepted upon himself every accident that might happen.
In the end, they diverted a river through it.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא גַּבְרָא דְּזַבֵּין אַרְעָא לְחַבְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new story. Like the lion case, it asks whether a general phrase covers rare events.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the case: a seller accepted every accident, and then an unusual accident (a river diverted through the land) happened.

steps.title: רבינא rules that the seller must pay
steps.stepSummary: The case came to רבינא, who told the seller to pay the buyer because he had accepted every accident.
steps.simpleTranslation: He came before רבינא. רבינא told the seller: Go and satisfy him (pay him), because you took upon yourself every accident that might happen.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא gives his ruling: the seller has to pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא reads the promise exactly as it was said. 'Every accident' means every accident, including a rare one like this.

keyTerms.meaning: Go satisfy him, meaning pay him back
רבינא, an אמורא

phrases.english: He came before רבינא,
he said to him: Go satisfy him,
phrases.notes: רבינא is talking to the seller and telling him to pay the buyer.

phrases.english: since you accepted upon yourself
every accident that might happen.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲתָא לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרָבִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first ruling on the story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The seller pays, because the wording 'every accident' includes even a rare one.

steps.title: רב אחא בר תחליפא: this is a rare accident
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בר תחליפא challenges רבינא: an uncommon accident like this is not covered.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא בר תחליפא said to רבינא: This is an accident that is not common!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא בר תחליפא pushes back on רבינא's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His point is that when the seller said 'every accident,' he only meant the usual kinds. A river diverted through a field is so rare that the seller never thought of it, so he should not have to pay.

keyTerms.meaning: That is not common
רב אחא בר תחליפא, an אמורא

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בַּר תַּחְלִיפָא לְרָבִינָא:
phrases.english: רב אחא בר תחליפא said to רבינא:
It is an uncommon accident!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בַּר תַּחְלִיפָא לְרָבִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבינא's ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבינא's ruling that the seller must pay.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A general promise only covers accidents that people expect. A rare accident falls outside what the seller meant.

steps.title: The case reaches רבא, who agrees it is a rare accident
steps.stepSummary: The case moved on and reached רבא. He ruled that it is an uncommon accident, so the seller is not responsible.
steps.simpleTranslation: The matter was passed along and came before רבא. He said to them: It is an uncommon accident.
steps.whatsHappening: A higher authority, רבא, decides the case, and he sides with רב אחא בר תחליפא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא agrees that wide wording does not stretch to rare disasters. So the seller does not have to pay, which goes against רבינא's ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: The matter rolled along, meaning the case was passed on
And it reached

phrases.english: The matter rolled along,
and it reached רבא.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: אוּנְסָא דְּלָא שְׁכִיחַ הוּא.
phrases.english: He said to them: It is an uncommon accident.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיגַּלְגַּל מִילְּתָא וּמְטָא לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבא decides in favor of רב אחא בר תחליפא's view.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A promise to cover 'every accident' does not include a rare accident, so the seller does not pay.

steps.title: רבינא challenges רבא from the conditional גט
steps.stepSummary: רבינא quotes the ברייתא: in the case of 'if I do not get up from this illness,' a house falling or a snakebite still makes the גט valid. That seems to show that rare accidents are included.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא challenged רבא: 'If I do not get up from this illness,' and a house fell on him or a snake bit him, it is a valid גט!
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא defends his first ruling by challenging רבא with the ברייתא from Step 9.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A house falling down and a snakebite are uncommon accidents. Yet the ברייתא counts them as part of the husband's general words, and the גט works. So rare events should also be covered by the seller's general promise, and the seller should pay.

keyTerms.meaning: He challenged him from an earlier source
A snake bit him
I will get up from this illness

steps.confusionAlert: This is the second case of the ברייתא from Step 9, the 'if I do not get up' case, where the גט IS valid. It is not the 'if I die from this illness' case, where it is not.

phrases.english: רבינא challenged רבא:
'If I do not get up from this illness,'
and a house fell on him
or a snake bit him,
this is a valid גט!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵיתִיבֵיהּ רָבִינָא לְרָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבא's ruling using the ברייתא from Step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's rule that a general promise does not cover rare accidents.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the ברייתא, rare accidents (a house falling, a snakebite) are included in the husband's general words. So rare accidents should be included in the seller's general promise too.

steps.title: רבא points to the first half of the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers רבינא: the first half (רישא) of the same ברייתא says that a rare accident makes it 'not a גט,' which suggests rare accidents are NOT included.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: But you can just as easily learn from the first half of the ברייתא, where it says that it is not a גט!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes back on רבינא's proof by showing that the first half of the same ברייתא seems to point the other way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the רישא, the husband said 'this is a גט if I die from this illness,' and then he died when a house fell on him or a snake bit him. The ברייתא rules it is not a גט, which suggests his condition did not count rare accidents. So the רישא and the סיפא pull in opposite directions, and the proof from the סיפא no longer stands on its own.

keyTerms.meaning: 'But say...': introduces another way to read the source
The first part of a משנה or ברייתא
It is not a valid divorce document

steps.confusionAlert: Both halves of the ברייתא are about the same kinds of accidents: a house falling and a snakebite. The difference is the husband's wording. In the רישא he said 'if I die from this illness,' and in the סיפא he said 'if I do not get up from this illness.'

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
But say from the first clause: it is not a bill of divorce!
phrases.notes: The first clause is the case where he said 'if I die from this illness' and then a house fell on him or a snake bit him.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵימָא מֵרֵישָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof רבינא brought in Step 16 from the סיפא of the ברייתא.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof from the ברייתא entirely, without proving the opposite.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The רישא of the same ברייתא suggests the opposite conclusion, so the ברייתא cannot decide the question.

steps.title: Does a contradiction cancel the proof?
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא מדפתי asks רבינא: just because the first half clashes with the second half, can we no longer use the ברייתא to raise a challenge?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא מדפתי said to רבינא: Because the רישא contradicts the סיפא, does that mean we can no longer raise a challenge from this ברייתא?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא מדפתי questions רבא's move. He asks whether a clash inside a ברייתא is really enough to throw out a proof from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אחא מדפתי thinks the סיפא might still be good evidence even if the רישא is hard to explain. His question is about method: when a source contradicts itself, is it still usable?

keyTerms.meaning: The last part of a משנה or ברייתא
It is difficult; there is a contradiction
We raise a refutation or challenge

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא מִדִּפְתִּי לְרָבִינָא:
phrases.english: Rav Aḥa of Difti said to Ravina:
And because the first clause contradicts the latter clause,
we cannot raise an objection from it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִשּׁוּם דְּקַשְׁיָא רֵישָׁא אַסֵּיפָא לָא מוֹתְבִינַן תְּיוּבְתָּא מִינַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions whether רבא's rejection in Step 17 is really valid.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's claim that the clash between the רישא and the סיפא cancels the proof.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A contradiction inside a source may not be enough reason to ignore the clear statement in the סיפא.

steps.title: The ברייתא is unreliable, so follow logic
steps.stepSummary: רבינא agrees: since the two halves contradict each other, this ברייתא was not taught in the בית מדרש and its text is faulty. So we follow plain reasoning.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Yes. Since the רישא contradicts the סיפא, it was not taught in the בית מדרש, and it is a faulty text. Go after logic.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא answers that a ברייתא that contradicts itself cannot be trusted. We decide the question with common-sense reasoning instead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא had brought the proof himself, but now he admits it does not work. Without a reliable source, plain logic says a person who accepts 'every accident' does not have truly unusual events in mind. That supports רבא's ruling that the seller is not responsible.

keyTerms.meaning: Yes
The study hall, where reliable teachings were reviewed and taught
A faulty, corrupted version of a teaching
Logical reasoning

steps.whatToRemember: A ברייתא that contradicts itself is treated as unreliable, so we follow סברא. Here סברא says an uncommon accident is not included in 'every accident.'
steps.whyThisMatters: This closes the river case in favor of רבא: a seller who accepted every accident is not responsible for a rare one like a diverted river.

phrases.english: He said to him: Yes,
phrases.notes: The one answering here is רבינא, the same person who brought the proof in the first place.

phrases.english: since the first clause contradicts the latter clause,
it was not stated in the study hall,
and it is corrupted;
go after reason.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אִין כֵּיוָן דְּקַשְׁיָא רֵישָׁא אַסֵּיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אחא מדפתי's question from Step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rejects the source as unreliable and falls back on logic.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might think the סיפא of the ברייתא is still good evidence even though it clashes with the רישא.
steps.terutzMaskana: A self-contradicting ברייתא is faulty, so we follow סברא, which says rare accidents are not included.

steps.title: Sailors accept every accident, then the river is blocked
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא and רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע bought sesame by the נהר מלכא and hired sailors who accepted every accident. Then the river was dammed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא and רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע bought sesame on the bank of the נהר מלכא. They hired sailors to carry it across, and the sailors accepted responsibility for any accident that might happen. In the end, the נהר מלכא was dammed up...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story on the same topic of accepting 'every accident.' It is setting up a ruling that will come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sailors promised to cover any accident that might happen. Then the river was blocked, so the sesame could not be shipped. The question being set up is whether a blocked river counts as an accident the sailors promised to cover.

keyTerms.meaning: Sesame
Sailors or boatmen
An accident beyond one's control
Was dammed up or blocked

phrases.aramaic: רַב פָּפָּא וְרַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ
phrases.english: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua,
bought sesame on the bank of the Malka River.
They hired sailors to carry it across,
and they accepted upon themselves any accident that might occur.
In the end, the Malka River was dammed,

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פָּפָּא וְרַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ זְבֻן שׁוּמְשְׁמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a new real-life case that tests the rule just reached in Step 19.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling yet; this sets up a case where sailors accepted every accident and the river was then dammed.

steps.title: The buyers demand donkeys from the sailors
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא and רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע tell the sailors to hire donkeys to carry the sesame, because the sailors accepted every accident.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to the sailors: Hire donkeys and bring them to us, because you accepted responsibility for any accident that happens!
steps.whatsHappening: The story from the last step continues. The two buyers claim that the sailors must still deliver the sesame, by donkey if needed. This sets up the ruling of רבא that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyers read the sailors' promise very broadly: 'every accident' should include even a dammed river. This is the same question the גמרא has been asking, whether a general promise covers rare accidents.

keyTerms.meaning: Donkeys (or donkey drivers)
Release them to us, meaning make them available to us
An accident outside a person's control
You took upon yourselves (you accepted responsibility)

phrases.english: They said to them:
phrases.notes: רב פפא and רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע are speaking to the sailors they hired.

phrases.english: Hire donkeys and release them to us,
phrases.notes: They mean: get donkeys to carry the sesame overland, since the boats can't go.

phrases.english: for you accepted upon yourselves
any accident that might arise!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לְהוּ: אֱגוּרוּ חַמָּרֵי אַפְקְעִינְהוּ נִיהֲלַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story begun in step 20 by giving the buyers' claim after the river was dammed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The buyers claim that the sailors' acceptance of 'every accident' obligates them to deliver the goods by donkey.

steps.title: רבא rules that a dammed river is a rare accident
steps.stepSummary: רבא rebukes the two חכמים and rules that a dammed river is a rare accident, which the sailors never accepted.
steps.simpleTranslation: They came before רבא. He said to them: You white geese who strip people of their cloaks! This is an uncommon accident.
steps.whatsHappening: The case goes to רבא, who rules against the buyers. He says the sailors don't have to pay, because a dammed river is a rare accident.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ruling settles the question of the סוגיא. Someone who accepts 'every accident' is responsible only for common accidents, not rare ones. רבא sharply criticizes the חכמים for trying to take money that was not theirs.

keyTerms.meaning: White geese
Cloaks
A rare, uncommon accident

steps.whatToRemember: A person who accepts responsibility for 'every accident' is not responsible for rare accidents. A dammed river is a rare accident.
steps.whyThisMatters: It gives a practical ruling for the question discussed since step 12: a general acceptance of accidents does not cover rare accidents.

phrases.english: They came before Rava;
he said to them:
White geese,
phrases.notes: A sharp nickname, pointing at their long white beards: old and wise, yet acting unfairly.

phrases.english: who strip people of their cloaks!
It is an uncommon accident.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲתוֹ לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרָבָא, אֲמַר לְהוּ: קָאקֵי חִיוָּרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the claim made in step 21 and decides the case.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Accepting 'every accident' does not include a rare accident such as a river being dammed, so the sailors are exempt.

steps.title: New משנה: she may be alone with him only before witnesses
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a woman whose sick husband gave her a conditional גט may not be alone with him except in front of witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: She may not be alone with him except in front of witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It sets a rule for the woman who received a גט from her sick husband that takes effect if he dies: she may be alone with him only when witnesses are present.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Her status is unclear until we know whether he dies from this illness. If they lived together as husband and wife during this time, it could cause problems for the גט. So the משנה requires witnesses whenever they are together.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מתניתין, our משנה
She may not be alone together (the איסור of יחוד)
In front of witnesses

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a general rule about all married couples. It applies to the woman who received a גט from her sick husband on condition that he dies from this illness.

phrases.english: MISHNA: She may not be secluded with him
phrases.notes: 'She' is the wife and 'him' is the sick husband who gave her a גט that works if he dies from this illness.

phrases.english: except in the presence of witnesses,

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ לֹא תִּתְיַיחֵד עִמּוֹ אֶלָּא בִּפְנֵי עֵדִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה after the conclusion of the previous sugya.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A woman holding a conditional גט from her sick husband may be alone with him only in front of witnesses.

steps.title: Even a slave counts, except her own maidservant
steps.stepSummary: The משנה adds that even a male or female slave is enough, but not the wife's own maidservant, because she feels too comfortable around her.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even in front of a male slave, even in front of a maidservant, except her own maidservant, because she is very comfortable with her maidservant.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה explains who counts as a 'witness' for this rule. A male or female slave is enough, but her personal maidservant is not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the 'witnesses' are not there to testify in court. They are there so the couple won't come close to each other. Most slaves achieve this, but a woman feels so comfortable with her own maidservant that her presence would not stop her.

keyTerms.meaning: A male slave
A female slave (maidservant)
She is very comfortable and familiar with her
Except for

steps.whatToRemember: For this יחוד rule, even a slave counts as a witness, except the wife's own maidservant, whom she is too used to.

phrases.english: even in the presence of a slave,
even in the presence of a maidservant;
except for her own maidservant,
because she is familiar with
phrases.notes: Literally 'her heart is coarse with her': she is so used to her that she won't hold back in front of her.

phrases.english: her maidservant.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲפִילּוּ עַל פִּי עֶבֶד אֲפִילּוּ עַל פִּי שִׁפְחָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains who counts as a 'witness' under the rule of step 23 and gives one exception.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A male or female slave is enough to prevent יחוד, except the wife's own maidservant.

steps.title: What is the wife's status in the waiting days
steps.stepSummary: The משנה asks whether the wife counts as married or divorced during the days between getting the conditional גט and her husband's death. It then opens רבי יהודה's answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is her status during those days? רבי יהודה says:
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה asks a new question: during the days after she got the גט but before her husband died, what is her status? It is setting up the answer, which starts with רבי יהודה and continues in the next section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the משנה dealt with a practical rule: she may not be alone with him without witnesses. Now it asks the bigger question behind that rule. If he later dies, the גט takes effect, so it is unclear whether during the waiting time she should be treated as a married woman or as divorced.

keyTerms.meaning: What is she? Here it means: what is her legal status
During those days, the waiting time before the husband dies
רבי יהודה says; opens his opinion

steps.confusionAlert: The answer is not given here. 'רבי יהודה says' only opens his opinion, and what he actually rules comes in the next section.

phrases.english: What is she during those days?
phrases.notes: 'Those days' means the time after she got the גט but before her husband died.

phrases.english: רבי יהודה says:

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה הִיא בְּאוֹתָן הַיָּמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the practical rule about being alone with witnesses to the wife's basic status during the waiting period.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the wife counts as married or divorced during the days between getting the conditional גט and her husband's death.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The answer begins with רבי יהודה and continues in the next section.
